newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico soybean plantings woefully low, imports up.
newsitem.headline: Mexico soybean plantings woefully low, imports up.

text.p: Mexican soybean plantings are woefully low this year even though recent rains ended a prolonged drought, soybean sources said Wednesday.

The local office of American Soybean Association (ASA) said in a report that as little as 6,000 hectares have been planted in southern Tamaulipas, the traditional top growing state and favored region within the state.
"We were able to confirm that there are less than 10,000 hectares of soybeans in southern Tamaulipas, probably as little as 6,000 hectares," ASA said.
That does not augur well for the national crop which has been on a dramatic decline in recent years because of water shortages and yield-lowering white fly infestation.
Early season expectations were for the national crop to dip to no more than 65,000 tonnes, down from 165,000 tonnes in 1995. But now those forecasts look far too high.

Even local Agriculture Ministry officials estimate that in the whole of Tamaulipas only 30,000 hectares have been planted, which, with expectations of yields of one tonne per hectare, will bring in a crop of around 30,000 tonnes.

Adding to the poor crop poor crop outlook, although opening doors for more import opportunities, are predictions from the ASA that there is little prospect for soybeans to be planted in other Mexican states.

"There is no indication that those farmers (from Sonora and Sinaloa) will plant any soybean this (1997) spring and there is no indication that soybeans will be planted in the summer of 1997 in Chihuahua either," the ASA said.

The ASA also noted the tendency for Tamaulipas farmers to switch to other crops, such as vegetables, cotton and sorghum rather than soybeans, especially because the recent rains gave them more options on un-irrigated fields.
"Farmers in the (Tamaulipas) area are waiting for the water to subside in order to go in and plant sorghum, which can be practically planted at any time of the year in that area," ASA said.

Gonzalo Cardenas Jimenez, chairman of Guadalajara-based Chamber of Western Edible Oil Manufacturers, told Reuters recently he expected output to fall to 50,000 tonnes this calendar year from the 135,000 tonnes he estimated the national crop produced in 1995.

"Mexico will have its lowest ever soybean harvest," Cardenas predicted, blaming the dramatic reduction from a 1989 peak of 942,400 tonnes on the drought that Mexico hyad suffered up to three months ago.
Cardenas expects imports to rise to 2.6 million tonnes in the Sept 1-Aug 31 1996-1997 cycle, up from his preliminary estimate of 2.23 million tonnes in the cycle that has just ended.

ASA reckons those figures a little too conservative. "It now looks feasibly that we could have 2.7 million tonnes of imports in this marketing year," the U.S. promotions group said, boosting its forecast from an original 2.3 million tonnes.

The most recent U.S. Department of Agriculture update had imports from the United States at 2,573,000 tonnes to August 21, with 10 days of the cycle remaining. Mexico imports 95 percent of its soybean needs from the United States and the remainder other nations, normally Brazil.
Mexico imported a record 2,229,188 tonnes in the 1995 calendar year, according to the Agriculture Ministry.
